uni-msc-maths-a.title: M.Sc Mathematics I · Analysis, Algebra & Numerical Methods
uni-msc-maths-a.description: Graduate M.Sc Mathematics core: real and complex analysis (uniform convergence, Lebesgue integration, residues), abstract algebra (groups, Sylow theory, rings and fields) and numerical methods with code labs. Goes beyond uni-bsc-maths.

courses.title: Abstract Algebra (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Groups and permutation groups, Lagrange and Sylow theorems, rings, ideals and finite fields, with counting problems and a code lab on multiplicative orders.
outcomes: Learners can count elements by cycle type in Sₙ
Learners can use Sylow theorems to constrain group structure
Learners can compute unit groups of ℤₙ and build finite fields
Learners can code multiplicative order computations

scenes.text: Aditya studies every way to rearrange four cards: 24 permutations.
He asks: how many shuffles undo themselves when done twice?

steps.title: Lagrange and orders
steps.body:
For finite G and subgroup H, |H| divides |G| (cosets partition G). Hence the order of any element divides |G|.

In Sₙ the order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths.

steps.title: Solved example · elements of order 2 in S₄
steps.body:
Order 2 means cycle type (2) or (2,2).
- Transpositions: C(4,2) = 6
- Double transpositions: 3
Total **9**.

steps.title: Solved example · order of (1 2 3)(4 5)
steps.body: lcm(3,2) = 6. In S₅ the maximum element order is 6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The converse of Lagrange is false: A₄ (order 12) has no subgroup of order 6.
- Multiplying cycle lengths instead of taking the lcm.

activity.prompt: How many elements of order 2 are there in the symmetric group S₄?

quiz.q: A₄ has no subgroup of order
quiz.why: Classic counterexample to converse of Lagrange.

story.title: Is there a simple group of order 168?

scenes.text: GL(3,2) has order 168 and is simple. Priya checks what Sylow forces.
The number of Sylow 7-subgroups cannot be 1 — so it must be 8.

steps.title: The theorems
steps.body: |G| = pᵃm with p∤m. Then Sylow p-subgroups (order pᵃ) exist, are all conjugate, and their number nₚ satisfies **nₚ ≡ 1 (mod p)** and **nₚ | m**. nₚ = 1 ⇔ the Sylow subgroup is normal.

steps.title: Solved example · order 15
steps.body: n₃ | 5, n₃ ≡ 1 mod 3 → n₃ = 1. n₅ | 3, ≡ 1 mod 5 → 1. Both normal, so G ≅ ℤ₃×ℤ₅ ≅ ℤ₁₅: every group of order 15 is cyclic.

steps.title: Solved example · order 168
steps.body: 168 = 2³·3·7. n₇ | 24 and n₇ ≡ 1 mod 7 → n₇ ∈ {1, 8}. Simple ⇒ n₇ ≠ 1 ⇒ **n₇ = 8**, giving 8×6 = 48 elements of order 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using nₚ | |G| instead of nₚ | m (both true, but the second is sharper).
- Forgetting that distinct subgroups of prime order intersect trivially (needed for element counting).

activity.prompt: In a simple group of order 168, how many Sylow 7-subgroups are there?

lessons.title: Lab: Rings, units and finite fields

scenes.text: Reed–Solomon codes in QR codes compute in the field GF(2⁸) with 256 elements.
To understand them, Karan first studies ℤₙ and polynomial quotient rings.

steps.title: Units and ideals
steps.body:
In ℤₙ, a is a unit iff gcd(a,n)=1, so |ℤₙˣ| = φ(n). ℤₙ is a field iff n is prime.

In a commutative ring R: R/I is a field ⇔ I is maximal; R/I is an integral domain ⇔ I is prime.

steps.title: Solved example · GF(8)
steps.body: x³+x+1 has no root in GF(2) (f(0)=1, f(1)=1), so it is irreducible and GF(2)[x]/(x³+x+1) is a field with 2³ = 8 elements; its multiplicative group is cyclic of order 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'No roots ⇒ irreducible' only works for degree 2 and 3.
- ℤ₄ is not GF(4): ℤ₄ has a zero divisor (2·2=0).

activity.prompt: How many units does the ring ℤ₃₆ have?

quiz.why: ℤ[x]/(x) ≅ ℤ, a domain but not a field.
Finite subgroup of a field's units is cyclic.

scenes.text: A crypto intern needs a generator of ℤₚˣ.
She writes a short program to compute the multiplicative order of a mod n.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: ord_n(a) is the least k ≥ 1 with aᵏ ≡ 1 mod n (requires gcd(a,n)=1). It divides φ(n). a is a primitive root iff ord = φ(n).

steps.title: Efficient check
steps.body: Only test k = φ(n)/q for prime factors q of φ(n): a is primitive iff a^{φ(n)/q} ≢ 1 for all q.

activity.prompt: Read two integers a and n from one line and print the multiplicative order of a modulo n (assume gcd(a,n)=1).
activity.starter:
a, n = map(int, input().split())
# compute smallest k>=1 with pow(a,k,n)==1
activity.solution:
a, n = map(int, input().split())
k, x = 1, a % n
while x != 1:
    x = x * a % n
    k += 1
print(k)
activity.hint: Keep multiplying by a modulo n until you get back to 1.

courses.title: Real & Complex Analysis (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Uniform convergence and its consequences, Lebesgue measure and integration, and contour integration by residues, with full proofs sketched and worked integrals.
outcomes: Learners can test uniform convergence with the sup-norm
Learners can compute Lebesgue integrals of functions altered on null sets
Learners can evaluate real integrals by the residue theorem
Learners can evaluate trigonometric integrals on the unit circle

scenes.text: Sana notices fₙ(x)=xⁿ is continuous on [0,1] for every n, yet the limit jumps to 1 at x=1.
Her professor smiles: 'Pointwise limits can break continuity. Uniform ones cannot.'

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
fₙ → f **pointwise** on E if for each x and ε>0 there is N(ε,x).

fₙ → f **uniformly** if N depends only on ε, equivalently **Mₙ = sup_E |fₙ−f| → 0**.

Theorems: a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous; ∫ and lim can be swapped on [a,b] under uniform convergence; Weierstrass M-test: |uₙ| ≤ Mₙ with ΣMₙ<∞ ⇒ Σuₙ converges uniformly.

steps.title: Solved example · xⁿ
steps.body:
On [0,1): f=0 pointwise, but sup|xⁿ| = 1 for every n → **not uniform**.
On [0,½]: sup = (½)ⁿ → 0 → **uniform**.

steps.title: Solved example · moving bump
steps.body: fₙ(x)= nx/(1+n²x²) on [0,1]. Pointwise limit 0. Derivative zero at x=1/n where fₙ = ½. So Mₙ = ½ for all n → not uniform, even though the limit is continuous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding uniform convergence because the limit is continuous (converse of the theorem is false; Dini's theorem needs monotonicity and compactness).
- Checking a few points instead of computing the supremum.

activity.prompt: Classify each sequence on the stated set.

options: monotone sequence, continuous limit, compact domain

scenes.text: Ravi's f equals 1 on rationals and x² on irrationals. Riemann sums never settle.
Lebesgue says: the rationals have measure zero — ignore them.

steps.title: Measure zero and a.e.
steps.body:
Any countable set has Lebesgue measure 0: cover qₖ by an interval of length ε/2ᵏ, total ≤ ε.

If f = g almost everywhere then ∫f = ∫g.

steps.title: Convergence theorems
steps.body:
- **Monotone convergence:** 0 ≤ fₙ ↑ f ⇒ ∫fₙ → ∫f.
- **Fatou:** ∫ lim inf fₙ ≤ lim inf ∫fₙ.
- **Dominated convergence:** fₙ → f a.e., |fₙ| ≤ g ∈ L¹ ⇒ ∫fₙ → ∫f.

steps.title: Solved example · Ravi's function
steps.body: f = x² a.e. on [0,1], so ∫f dm = ∫₀¹x²dx = **1/3**.

steps.title: Solved example · DCT
steps.body: lim ∫₀¹ n x/(1+n²x²) dx: integrand → 0 pointwise; but dominated convergence needs a bound. Direct: ∫ = (1/2n)ln(1+n²) → 0. So the limit is 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking measure zero means finite or empty (the Cantor set is uncountable with measure 0).
- Applying DCT without an integrable dominating function (fₙ = n·1_(0,1/n) is a counterexample: ∫fₙ = 1 but fₙ → 0).

activity.prompt: f(x)=1 if x is rational, f(x)=x² otherwise, on [0,1]. Compute its Lebesgue integral (3 decimals).

scenes.text: An engineer needs ∫ dx/(1+x²)² over ℝ for a filter's energy.
Close the contour in the upper half-plane and only one residue matters.

steps.title: Residue theorem
steps.body:
For f analytic inside and on a closed contour C except isolated singularities zₖ: ∮_C f dz = 2πi Σ Res(f,zₖ).

Pole of order m: Res = (1/(m−1)!) lim d^{m−1}/dz^{m−1}[(z−z₀)ᵐ f(z)].

steps.title: Solved example · ∫dx/(1+x²)²
steps.body:
Upper pole z=i, order 2. g(z)=(z+i)⁻², g'(i) = −2(2i)⁻³ = −2/(−8i) = 1/(4i).
Semicircle contribution → 0 (|f| ~ R⁻⁴). Integral = 2πi·1/(4i) = **π/2 ≈ 1.5708**.

steps.title: Solved example · ∫dx/(1+x²)
steps.body: Simple pole at i, residue 1/(2i): integral = π.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including poles from the lower half-plane.
- Forgetting to show the arc integral vanishes (Jordan's lemma for e^{ix} integrands).

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(1+x²)² by residues (4 decimals).

quiz.why: Coefficient of z² in e^z is ½.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · trigonometric integrals on the unit circle

scenes.text: An astrophysics student needs ∫₀^{2π} dθ/(5+4cosθ) to average over an elliptic orbit.
Substituting z = e^{iθ} turns it into a contour integral around |z|=1.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: z=e^{iθ}: cosθ = (z+z⁻¹)/2, dθ = dz/(iz). Then pick only poles inside |z|<1.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
∫ dθ/(5+4cosθ) = ∮ dz/(iz(5+2z+2/z)) = ∮ dz/(i(2z²+5z+2)) = ∮ dz/(i(2z+1)(z+2)).
Inside: z = −½, residue 1/(i·2·(3/2)) = 1/(3i). Integral = 2πi/(3i) = **2π/3 ≈ 2.0944**.
General: ∫₀^{2π} dθ/(a+b cosθ) = 2π/√(a²−b²), a>|b|.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/(iz) Jacobian.
- Taking the pole at z=−2, which lies outside the unit circle.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀^{2π} dθ/(5+4cosθ) (4 decimals).

scenes.text: 'State Sylow's theorems and show every group of order 15 is cyclic.'
Clear statements, then the key step, then the conclusion.

steps.title: Oral proof structure
steps.body:
- State the theorem precisely, including hypotheses.
- Give the one idea that drives the proof.
- Offer a counterexample showing a hypothesis is needed.

steps.title: Hypothesis matters
steps.body: Dominated convergence fails for fₙ = n·1_(0,1/n): no integrable dominating function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping hypotheses (compactness, continuity).
- Waving hands at 'clearly'.

rounds.q: Why does uniform convergence preserve continuity but pointwise does not?
rounds.model: Given ε, uniform convergence gives one N for all x, so |f(x)−f(y)| ≤ |f−f_N|(x) + |f_N(x)−f_N(y)| + |f_N−f|(y) < ε near y. Pointwise, N depends on x and the argument fails, e.g. xⁿ on [0,1].

rounds.q: Show every group of order 15 is cyclic.
rounds.model: Sylow gives n₃ | 5 with n₃ ≡ 1 mod 3, so n₃ = 1; similarly n₅ = 1. Both Sylow subgroups are normal, intersect trivially and generate G, so G ≅ ℤ₃ × ℤ₅ ≅ ℤ₁₅.
followups: Is every group of order 21 cyclic?

rounds.q: Explain the residue theorem and use it for ∫dx/(1+x²).
rounds.model: Close the real line with a large upper semicircle; the arc integral vanishes since |f| ~ 1/R². The only enclosed pole is i with residue 1/(2i), so the integral is 2πi·1/(2i) = π.

rounds.q: Why is Newton's method quadratically convergent?
rounds.model: Expanding f(r) about x_k and subtracting the Newton step gives e_{k+1} = (f''(ξ)/2f'(x_k)) e_k², so with f'(r) ≠ 0 the error squares each step.
followups: What happens at a double root?

scenes.text: Nikhil interviews for a quant analyst role and a PhD position in the same month.
Both ask for clear thinking under pressure.

steps.title: Think aloud
steps.body: Interviewers grade the reasoning path. Say your plan, compute, then sanity-check.

steps.title: Classic puzzle
steps.body: Expected number of fair coin tosses to get two heads in a row: E = 6 (set up states 0 and H).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Not checking with a simple case.

rounds.q: Expected tosses of a fair coin until HH?
rounds.model: Let E be expected from start and F after one H. E = 1 + ½F + ½E and F = 1 + ½·0 + ½E. Solving gives E = 6.

rounds.q: Explain the condition number to a non-mathematician.
rounds.model: It measures how much a small error in the data can be magnified in the answer; κ = 10⁸ means you may lose about eight digits of accuracy.

rounds.q: Tell us about a proof you struggled with and how you finished it.
rounds.model: Name the result, describe the failed attempt, the insight or reference that unlocked it, and the habit learned (e.g. trying small cases first).
followups: How do you read a paper?

rounds.model: Connect two concrete strengths to the role with evidence (project, ranking, code) and show what you want to learn next.

scenes.text: Your thesis chapter needs a clean proof that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
Order the steps.

steps.title: Template
steps.body: Fix point and ε → choose N from uniform convergence → choose δ from continuity of f_N → triangle inequality → conclude.

steps.title: Style
steps.body: One idea per sentence; name every quantifier.

steps.title: Pitfall
steps.body: Choosing δ before N makes δ depend on the wrong function.

activity.prompt: Order the proof that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous at x₀.
items: By uniform convergence pick N with |f_N − f| < ε/3 everywhere
By continuity of f_N pick δ with |f_N(x) − f_N(x₀)| < ε/3 when |x − x₀| < δ
Apply the triangle inequality through f_N(x) and f_N(x₀)
Conclude |f(x) − f(x₀)| < ε, so f is continuous at x₀

courses.title: Numerical Methods (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Root finding, numerical quadrature, linear systems and ODE solvers with error analysis and Python labs.
outcomes: Learners can implement Newton–Raphson and state its convergence order
Learners can apply Simpson's rule and estimate error

scenes.text: Deepa wonders how a chip computes √2 with only + − × ÷.
Newton's method doubles the number of correct digits each step.

steps.title: Method and convergence
steps.body: x_{k+1} = x_k − f(x_k)/f'(x_k). If f(r)=0, f'(r)≠0 and f is C², then e_{k+1} ≈ (f''(r)/2f'(r)) e_k² — **quadratic convergence**. For a multiple root convergence drops to linear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting near a stationary point (f'≈0) → divergence.
- Stopping on |x_{k+1}−x_k| alone without checking |f(x)|.

activity.prompt: Use Newton–Raphson on f(x)=x²−2 starting at x=1 until successive iterates differ by less than 1e-12. Print the root rounded to 6 decimals.
activity.solution:
x = 1.0
while True:
    nx = x - (x*x - 2)/(2*x)
    if abs(nx - x) < 1e-12:
        break
    x = nx
print(f'{nx:.6f}')

scenes.text: Mesh analysis of a two-loop circuit gives 2I₁+I₂=5 and I₁+3I₂=10.
Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting solves it — and scales to thousands of unknowns.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Forward elimination to upper triangular form (≈ 2n³/3 flops), then back substitution (n²). Partial pivoting swaps in the largest |pivot| to control round-off growth. LU = PA stores the multipliers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping pivoting with tiny pivots (e.g. 10⁻²⁰) → catastrophic error.
- Computing A⁻¹ to solve Ax=b (slower and less accurate).

scenes.text: A biologist models y' = y, y(0)=1 and wants y(0.1).
Euler gives 1.1; RK4 gets within 10⁻⁷ of e^{0.1}.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
Euler: y_{n+1} = yₙ + h f(tₙ,yₙ), global error O(h).
RK4: k₁=f(t,y), k₂=f(t+h/2, y+hk₁/2), k₃=f(t+h/2, y+hk₂/2), k₄=f(t+h, y+hk₃); y_{n+1} = yₙ + h(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6, global error O(h⁴).

Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using yₙ instead of yₙ + hk₂/2 in k₃.
- Explicit methods on stiff problems with too-large h → instability.

uni-msc-physics-a.description: Graduate-level M.Sc Physics core: quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics and classical electrodynamics with full derivations and computed numericals. Goes beyond the B.Sc Physics pack (uni-bsc-physics).

courses.title: Quantum Mechanics (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Postulates, bound states, the harmonic oscillator by ladder operators, the hydrogen atom and time-independent perturbation theory, at the depth of a standard M.Sc first-year course.
outcomes: Learners can solve the infinite well and compute energy levels in eV
Learners can derive the oscillator spectrum from ladder operators
Learners can use the hydrogen spectrum and its degeneracy
Learners can compute first-order perturbative energy shifts

scenes.text: Ananya grows CdSe nanocrystals and sees their colour shift from red to green as they shrink.
Her guide says: model the electron as a particle in a box and the colour shift falls out of one formula.

steps.title: Setting up the problem
steps.body:
V(x)=0 for 0<x<L and infinite outside. Inside, the time-independent Schrödinger equation is −(ħ²/2m)ψ''=Eψ, so ψ=A sin kx + B cos kx with k=√(2mE)/ħ.

Boundary conditions ψ(0)=0 gives B=0; ψ(L)=0 gives kL=nπ, n=1,2,3…

**Result:** Eₙ = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²) = n²h²/(8mL²), ψₙ=√(2/L) sin(nπx/L).

steps.title: Solved example · electron in a 1 nm box
steps.body:
- h²=(6.626×10⁻³⁴)²=4.390×10⁻⁶⁷ J²s²
- 8mL²=8×9.109×10⁻³¹×(10⁻⁹)²=7.287×10⁻⁴⁸
- E₁=6.03×10⁻²⁰ J = **0.376 eV**; E₂=4E₁=1.51 eV

The 1→2 transition needs 1.13 eV. Halving L quadruples every energy: smaller dots emit bluer light.

steps.title: Properties worth remembering
steps.body:
- n=0 is excluded: ψ would vanish everywhere, so the ground state has zero-point energy E₁>0 (uncertainty principle).
- ψₙ has n−1 nodes; states are orthonormal: ∫ψₘψₙdx=δₘₙ.
- ⟨x⟩=L/2 for every n; ⟨p⟩=0 but ⟨p²⟩=2mEₙ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ħ in h²/(8mL²) (or h in π²ħ²/2mL²) — off by 4π².
- Forgetting to convert joules to eV (divide by 1.602×10⁻¹⁹).
- Thinking energies scale as n — they scale as n².

activity.prompt: Compute the ground-state energy E₁ of an electron (m=9.109×10⁻³¹ kg) in an infinite well of width L=1.0 nm. Give your answer in eV.

lessons.title: Lab: Harmonic oscillator by ladder operators

scenes.text: Rahul measures the IR absorption of CO and sees nearly equally spaced vibrational lines.
Equal spacing is the fingerprint of a quantum harmonic oscillator.

steps.title: Algebraic method
steps.body:
H = p²/2m + ½mω²x². Define a = √(mω/2ħ)(x + ip/mω) and a† its adjoint. Using [x,p]=iħ one gets [a,a†]=1 and

**H = ħω(a†a + ½)**.

With N=a†a: [N,a]=−a and [N,a†]=a†, so a lowers and a† raises the eigenvalue of N by 1.

steps.title: Why the spectrum is (n+½)ħω
steps.body:
⟨ψ|N|ψ⟩=‖aψ‖²≥0, so lowering must stop at a state with a|0⟩=0. Then N|0⟩=0 and E₀=½ħω.

Raising: |n⟩=(a†)ⁿ|0⟩/√n!, with a†|n⟩=√(n+1)|n+1⟩ and a|n⟩=√n|n−1⟩. **Eₙ=(n+½)ħω.**

Solving a|0⟩=0 in position space gives the Gaussian ψ₀ ∝ exp(−mωx²/2ħ).

steps.title: Solved example · zero-point energy
steps.body:
ω=1.0×10¹⁴ rad/s: E₀=ħω/2=1.0546×10⁻³⁴×10¹⁴/2=5.27×10⁻²¹ J = **0.0329 eV**.

Compare kT at 300 K = 0.0259 eV: such a mode is only partly excited at room temperature.

steps.title: Solved example · ⟨x²⟩ in state |n⟩
steps.body:
x=√(ħ/2mω)(a+a†). Then x²=(ħ/2mω)(a²+a†²+aa†+a†a). Diagonal terms only: ⟨n|aa†+a†a|n⟩=2n+1.

**⟨x²⟩=(ħ/2mω)(2n+1)** — so ⟨V⟩=½mω²⟨x²⟩=½Eₙ (virial theorem).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a|n⟩=√(n+1)|n−1⟩ — the √(n+1) belongs to a†.

steps.title: Separating the equation
steps.body:
With V=−e²/(4πε₀r), write ψ=R(r)Yₗᵐ(θ,φ). The angular part gives L²Y=ħ²l(l+1)Y, L_zY=mħY.

The radial equation with u=rR has an effective potential V+ħ²l(l+1)/(2μr²). Normalisable solutions require n=n_r+l+1, giving

**Eₙ = −13.6 eV / n²** (independent of l and m — an accidental degeneracy from the hidden Runge–Lenz symmetry).

steps.title: Quantum numbers and degeneracy
steps.body:
- l = 0,…,n−1; m = −l,…,l
- Degeneracy without spin: Σ(2l+1) = **n²**; with spin 2n²

steps.title: The formulas
steps.body:
For H=H₀+λH' with non-degenerate unperturbed states |n⁰⟩:

- **First order:** Eₙ⁽¹⁾ = ⟨n⁰|H'|n⁰⟩
- **Second order:** Eₙ⁽²⁾ = Σₖ≠ₙ |⟨k⁰|H'|n⁰⟩|² / (Eₙ⁰ − Eₖ⁰)

The ground-state second-order shift is always negative (levels repel).

steps.title: Solved example · half-well step
steps.body:
H'=V₀ for 0<x<L/2. E⁽¹⁾ = (2/L)V₀∫₀^{L/2} sin²(nπx/L)dx = (2/L)V₀(L/4) = **V₀/2** for every n.

With V₀=0.20 eV the shift is 0.10 eV.

steps.body: H'=λx⁴ for the oscillator. Using x=√(ħ/2mω)(a+a†), ⟨0|(a+a†)⁴|0⟩=3, so E₀⁽¹⁾ = 3λ(ħ/2mω)².

- Trusting the series when ⟨k|H'|n⟩ is comparable to the level spacing.

courses.title: Statistical Mechanics (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Microcanonical counting, the canonical partition function, quantum statistics and the free electron gas, with computed numericals.
outcomes: Learners can count microstates and compute Boltzmann entropy
Learners can derive thermodynamics from a partition function
Learners can apply Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein distributions
Learners can compute the Fermi energy of a metal

scenes.text: Meera shakes 10 coins on a tray again and again and almost always gets close to five heads.
Not magic — there are far more arrangements near the middle. That counting is entropy.

steps.title: Microcanonical ensemble
steps.body:
An isolated system with fixed E, V, N: every accessible microstate is equally likely (postulate of equal a priori probabilities).

**S = k_B ln Ω(E,V,N)**, and 1/T = (∂S/∂E)_{V,N}.

steps.title: Solved example · coins / spins
steps.body:
N two-state units with n 'up': Ω = C(N,n).
- N=10, n=5: Ω = 252; n=10: Ω = 1.
- S(n=5) = k ln 252 = 5.53 k.

For N=100, C(100,50) ≈ 1.01×10²⁹ — the peak becomes razor sharp, which is why thermodynamics works.

steps.title: Solved example · Stirling and the two-state paramagnet
steps.body: Using ln N! ≈ N ln N − N, S/k = −N[x ln x + (1−x)ln(1−x)] with x=n/N. At x=½, S = Nk ln 2 (maximum). Beyond x=½ the energy rises while S falls → negative temperature, seen in nuclear spin systems.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using log base 10 in S = k ln Ω.
- Treating identical particles as distinguishable (Gibbs paradox: divide by N!).

activity.prompt: How many microstates Ω are there for 10 two-state spins with exactly 5 up?

quiz.why: Ω=2^N maximum total; per most probable macrostate S≈Nk ln 2.
Only bounded spectra let S decrease as E increases.

lessons.title: Lab: Canonical ensemble and the two-level system

scenes.text: Colour centres in diamond have two levels separated by ΔE.
Karthik needs the fraction excited at a given temperature — the canonical ensemble gives it at once.

steps.title: Partition function
steps.body:
System in contact with a reservoir at T: P(i) = e^{−βEᵢ}/Z, Z = Σ e^{−βEᵢ}, β=1/kT.

- F = −kT ln Z
- U = −∂ln Z/∂β
- S = (U−F)/T, C_V = ∂U/∂T

steps.title: Solved example · two levels 0 and ε
steps.body:
Z = 1 + e^{−βε}. Upper fraction p = 1/(e^{βε}+1).

If ε = kT: p = 1/(e+1) = **0.269**. U = εp; C_V shows a Schottky peak near kT ≈ 0.42ε.

steps.title: Solved example · equipartition
steps.body: Each quadratic term in H contributes ½kT. Diatomic gas at room temperature: 3 translational + 2 rotational → C_V = 5/2 R ≈ 20.8 J/mol K. Vibration is frozen out because ħω ≫ kT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting degeneracy factors gᵢ in Z.
- Applying equipartition to modes with ħω ≫ kT.

steps.title: Quantum distributions
steps.body:
Mean occupation of a single-particle state:
- Fermi–Dirac: n = 1/(e^{(ε−μ)/kT}+1)
- Bose–Einstein: n = 1/(e^{(ε−μ)/kT}−1)
- Classical limit (e^{(ε−μ)/kT} ≫ 1): Maxwell–Boltzmann.

steps.title: Free electron gas
steps.body:
Filling k-space spheres with 2 electrons per state: N = 2·(V/(2π)³)·(4/3)πk_F³ → k_F = (3π²n)^{1/3}

**E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^{2/3}**; average energy at T=0 is (3/5)E_F; electronic heat capacity ∝ T (only electrons within ~kT of E_F respond).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the spin factor 2 (gives 3π² → 6π²).
- Thinking photons have a conserved number: for photons μ = 0.

steps.body: Thermal wavelength λ = h/√(2πmkT). If nλ³ ≪ 1 the gas is classical (MB); if nλ³ ≳ 1 quantum statistics are required.

courses.title: Classical Electrodynamics (M.Sc)
courses.summary: Maxwell's equations and energy flow, waves in conductors, relativistic electrodynamics and guided waves with engineering-grade numericals.
outcomes: Learners can derive the wave equation and Poynting theorem
Learners can compute skin depth
Learners can use Lorentz transformations and four-vectors
Learners can compute waveguide cutoff frequencies

scenes.text: An ISRO intern sizes a solar sail. Sunlight near Earth carries 1361 W/m².
How strong is the electric field of that light? Poynting's theorem answers it.

steps.title: From Maxwell to waves
steps.body:
In vacuum: ∇·E=0, ∇·B=0, ∇×E=−∂B/∂t, ∇×B=μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t. Taking the curl of Faraday's law and using ∇×∇×E=∇(∇·E)−∇²E gives

**∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t²**, speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 2.998×10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Poynting theorem
steps.body:
−∂u/∂t = ∇·S + J·E with u = ½(ε₀E² + B²/μ₀) and **S = E×B/μ₀**.

For a plane wave, time-averaged intensity I = ½cε₀E₀². Radiation pressure: I/c (absorbed), 2I/c (reflected).

steps.title: Solved example · field in sunlight
steps.body:
E₀ = √(2I/(cε₀)) = √(2×1361/(2.998×10⁸×8.854×10⁻¹²)) = **1013 V/m**; B₀ = E₀/c = 3.38 μT.
Pressure on a perfect reflector: 2×1361/c = 9.1 μPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ for the time average of cos².
- Using E_rms in a formula built for amplitude E₀.

steps.title: Wave equation in a good conductor
steps.body:
With J=σE and σ ≫ ωε, ∇²E = μσ∂E/∂t. A solution e^{i(kz−ωt)} needs k² = iωμσ, so k = (1+i)/δ with

**δ = √(2/(ωμσ)) = √(2ρ/(ωμ))**. Fields decay as e^{−z/δ} and lag in phase.

steps.title: Solved example · copper at 60 Hz
steps.body:
ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω m, ω = 2π·60 = 377 rad/s, μ = 4π×10⁻⁷.
δ = √(3.36×10⁻⁸/(377×1.257×10⁻⁶)) = **8.4 mm**.
At 1 MHz δ ≈ 65 μm; at 10 GHz ≈ 0.65 μm — why microwave parts are silver/gold plated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using f instead of ω = 2πf.
- Forgetting δ ∝ 1/√f: 4× the frequency halves δ.

scenes.text: Cosmic-ray muons born 15 km up live only 2.2 μs — at best ~660 m of travel.
Yet detectors at sea level count many. Time dilation explains it, and the same Lorentz transform mixes E and B.

steps.title: Lorentz transformations
steps.body:
γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²). Coordinates: t' = γ(t − vx/c²), x' = γ(x − vt). Proper time intervals dilate: Δt = γΔτ.

Fields form the antisymmetric tensor F^{μν}; under a boost along x: E'_y = γ(E_y − vB_z), B'_z = γ(B_z − vE_y/c²). E·B and E²−c²B² are invariants.

steps.title: Solved example · magnetism as relativity
steps.body: A line charge λ at rest has only E. In a frame moving along it, the charge density becomes γλ and a current appears → a B field. Magnetism is the relativistic partner of electrostatics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying time dilation to the wrong frame: proper time is measured by the clock at rest with the event.
- Assuming E and B transform separately.

options: a clock at rest relative to the events

quiz.why: Since E²−c²B²>0 is invariant, a frame with B=0 exists.

steps.title: Modes and cutoff
steps.body:
In a hollow rectangular guide, TE_mn and TM_mn modes have

**f_c = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)²)**.

TE₁₀ has the lowest cutoff c/2a. Below f_c, fields are evanescent.

steps.title: Solved example · WR-90
steps.body: TE₁₀: f_c = 2.998×10⁸/(2×0.02286) = **6.56 GHz**. TE₂₀: 13.1 GHz. TE₀₁: c/2b = 14.8 GHz. So 8.2–12.4 GHz is single-mode.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- TM₁₀ and TM₀₁ do not exist in rectangular guides (both indices must be ≥1 for TM).
- Group velocity < c, phase velocity > c — no violation of relativity.

scenes.text: Three examiners, one blackboard. 'Derive it, don't recite it.'
Structure: state assumptions, write the key equation, check limits and units.

steps.title: How to answer a viva
steps.body:
- Start from the governing principle (Schrödinger, Maxwell, Boltzmann).
- Say what you assume and why.
- Finish with a limiting case or dimensional check.

steps.title: Sample limit check
steps.body: Fermi–Dirac → Maxwell–Boltzmann when e^{(ε−μ)/kT} ≫ 1; skin depth → ∞ as σ → 0 (insulator).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a formula without saying where it comes from.
- Freezing on a numeric: give an order of magnitude first.

rounds.q: Why does a quantum harmonic oscillator have zero-point energy?
rounds.model: The ladder method shows the spectrum is bounded below by a state annihilated by a, which has N=0 and energy ħω/2. Physically, confining x would cost momentum spread; minimising ⟨T⟩+⟨V⟩ subject to ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2 gives exactly ħω/2. The ground state is a minimum-uncertainty Gaussian.

rounds.q: Explain why energy levels of hydrogen are independent of l.
rounds.model: For a pure Coulomb potential the Runge–Lenz vector is conserved, enlarging the symmetry from SO(3) to SO(4); this extra symmetry ties different l values to the same n. Relativistic corrections and spin–orbit (fine structure) and the Lamb shift break it.

rounds.q: Derive the skin depth and tell me its value for copper at 50 Hz.
rounds.model: In a good conductor displacement current is negligible, so ∇²E = μσ ∂E/∂t. A plane-wave trial gives k=(1+i)/δ with δ=√(2/ωμσ). For copper at 50 Hz that is about 9.2 mm.

rounds.q: What is the physical meaning of the partition function?
rounds.model: Z sums the Boltzmann weights of all microstates; it measures how many states are effectively accessible at temperature T. All thermodynamics follows: F=−kT ln Z, U=−∂ln Z/∂β, and probabilities are weights over Z.
followups: What changes in the grand canonical ensemble?

scenes.text: A PhD admission panel asks about your project and why you chose physics research.
They test honesty, curiosity and how you handle being stuck.

steps.title: STAR for research stories
steps.body: Situation, Task, Action, Result — plus what you learned and what you would do differently.

steps.title: What panels look for
steps.body:
- You can explain your project to a non-specialist in one minute.
- You know its limitations.
- You have read 2–3 recent papers in the area.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Over-claiming results.
- Saying 'I have no weaknesses'.

rounds.q: Describe your M.Sc project in two minutes for a general physicist.
rounds.model: State the question and why it matters, the method you used, the key result with uncertainty, and one honest limitation plus the next step.
followups: What would you do with six more months?

rounds.q: Tell us about a time a calculation or experiment failed.
rounds.model: Describe the failure concretely, how you isolated the cause (units, sign, calibration), who you consulted, and the habit you now follow, e.g. dimensional checks at each step.
followups: How do you decide when to ask for help?

rounds.model: Give a specific question that excites you, show you understand research is slow and uncertain, and acknowledge industry options honestly.
followups: Where do you see yourself in five years?

rounds.q: A simulation gives a heat capacity that becomes negative. What do you check?
rounds.model: Check equilibration and sampling, compute C from ⟨E²⟩−⟨E⟩² to cross-check, verify sign and units, test known limits, and inspect finite-size effects before claiming new physics.
followups: When can C be negative physically?
